explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God tells Ezekiel to take a sharp sword and use it as a barber's razor to shave his head and beard (Ezekiel 5:1). A sword for a shave is a lot of trust in a steady hand. I'd keep my mustache far away from that appointment.

A staff makes a fine walking stick, but that's not what God names here. He tells Ezekiel to take a sharp sword and use it as a barber's razor (Ezekiel 5:1). The sword is the tool, and the shave is the job. I'm glad nobody asked me to shave with a staff either.

Measuring is close to the next part of the sign, but not to this part. God tells Ezekiel to use the sharp sword as a barber's razor on his head and beard (Ezekiel 5:1). Only after that does he take a set of scales. So the sword goes to the hair first, and the weighing comes second.
Scales it is. God says to take a set of scales and divide the hair (Ezekiel 5:1). Picture a prophet at the scales, sorting hair into three careful piles. That's a lot of focus for a haircut.

Baskets would hold the hair nicely, but God doesn't mention one. He says to take a set of scales and divide the hair (Ezekiel 5:1). Scales make the piles come out fair. I'd say the hair gets treated more carefully than my cookie dough ever has.

A jar is great for keeping things, but this sign is about dividing. God tells Ezekiel to take a set of scales and divide the hair (Ezekiel 5:1). The scales do the dividing. Nobody is jarring up a haircut here.
Right on target. God says to take a third and slash it with the sword all around the city (Ezekiel 5:2). The same sword that did the shaving now does the slashing. That's one busy sword for one sign.

No gate pile in this passage, friend. God says to take a third and slash it with the sword all around the city (Ezekiel 5:2). The sword that shaved the hair is the same one used on the second third. Sorry, gate pile, you didn't make the cut.

I can see why you'd think of tying something up, since a few strands do get secured later. But those are tucked in the folds of his garment (Ezekiel 5:3). For the second third, God says to slash it with the sword all around the city (Ezekiel 5:2). No cord is mentioned there.

True. God says to scatter a third to the wind, and adds, "For I will unleash a sword behind them." (Ezekiel 5:2) Burn one third, slash one third and scatter the last. Three piles, three different jobs.
This one is true, friend. God tells Ezekiel, "…you are to scatter a third to the wind." (Ezekiel 5:2) The first third is burned and the second is slashed. The last third goes to the wind.

Fire is right. God says to take a few of these strands, throw them into the fire, and burn them (Ezekiel 5:4). They had been tucked safely in his garment, so it's a surprising turn. Even a few strands get a part to play.

Water and hair do go together at bath time, but not here. God says to take a few of the strands and throw them into the fire, and burn them (Ezekiel 5:4). A well wouldn't burn anything. This sign calls for flames.

A pit is a good guess for a sign this serious, but God doesn't name one. He says to throw the few strands into the fire, and burn them (Ezekiel 5:4). The strands were tucked in his garment first. Then they go to the flames.

explanations.answer: To the whole house of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's what God says. A few strands are thrown into the fire, and "From there a fire will spread to the whole house of Israel." (Ezekiel 5:4) A handful of strands, and the reach is much bigger than the pile. That's a sobering picture.

God's words go wider than the city. He says the fire will spread to the whole house of Israel (Ezekiel 5:4). The city comes up with the second third of hair, which is slashed with the sword all around the city (Ezekiel 5:2). The fire from the few strands goes further.

The garment is where the few strands were secured, but it's not where the fire is headed. Ezekiel takes a few of them, throws them into the fire and burns them (Ezekiel 5:3-4). God says that from there a fire will spread to the whole house of Israel (Ezekiel 5:4). So the garment holds the strands, and the fire reaches far beyond it.

explanations.answer: She rebelled more wickedly than they did
explanations.explanation: That's how God puts it. Jerusalem "…has rebelled against My ordinances more wickedly than the nations…" (Ezekiel 5:6). She had been set in the center of the nations, with countries all around her (Ezekiel 5:5). That's a heavy thing to hear.

explanations.answer: She kept them better than they did
explanations.explanation: God says the opposite. She rebelled against His ordinances more wickedly than the nations, and against His statutes worse than the countries around her (Ezekiel 5:6). It's a hard word. Jerusalem was set right in the center of those nations (Ezekiel 5:5).

explanations.answer: She did about the same as they did
explanations.explanation: God doesn't call it even. He says she rebelled against His ordinances more wickedly than the nations, and against His statutes worse than the countries around her (Ezekiel 5:6). It's a sobering comparison. She wasn't just keeping pace with the nations.

True, and it's a hard line. God says, "…nor have you even conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you." (Ezekiel 5:7) The nations had ordinances of their own. Jerusalem didn't live up to those either.

This one is true, friend. God says, "…nor have you even conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you." (Ezekiel 5:7) He also says she was more insubordinate than the nations around her. It's a heavy word.
Not quite, friend. God says He will execute judgments among Jerusalem "…in the sight of the nations." (Ezekiel 5:8) So the nations will see it. Nothing here is hidden.

That's right. God says, "…I will execute judgments among you in the sight of the nations." (Ezekiel 5:8) The nations will see it. Later He says Jerusalem will be a ruin in the sight of all who pass by (Ezekiel 5:14).

explanations.answer: What He has never done before
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, "…I will do to you what I have never done before and will never do again." (Ezekiel 5:9) This is a heavy verse. The reason He gives is all her abominations.

explanations.answer: What He did in Noah's day
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't point back to any earlier event. God says He will do to Jerusalem "…what I have never done before and will never do again." (Ezekiel 5:9) So it's something new. It's a heavy word.

The verse doesn't name Sodom or any earlier event. God says, "…I will do to you what I have never done before and will never do again." (Ezekiel 5:9) That means something He hasn't done before. It's a heavy one.

God says the opposite. Because they defiled His sanctuary with their detestable idols and abominations, He says, "I will not look upon you with pity, nor will I spare you." (Ezekiel 5:11) He also says He will withdraw His favor. It's a heavy verse.

That's right. Because they defiled His sanctuary, God says He will withdraw His favor, and "I will not look upon you with pity, nor will I spare you." (Ezekiel 5:11) He says it as surely as He lives. It's a weighty word.
That's what the text says. A third of the people "…will die by plague or be consumed by famine within you…" (Ezekiel 5:12). This is a heavy part, friend. I think it's one to read slowly.

Flood and storm aren't in this verse. God says a third of the people will die by plague or be consumed by famine within the city (Ezekiel 5:12). It's a heavy line. The others are the sword outside the walls, and the scattering.

Neither earthquake nor hail shows up in the verse. God says a third will die by plague or be consumed by famine within the city (Ezekiel 5:12). It's a heavy part, friend. The next third falls by the sword outside the walls.
Yes. God says they "…will know that I, the LORD, in My zeal have spoken." (Ezekiel 5:13) It's His own word, spoken in His zeal. That's a heavy part, friend.

No king is named in this verse. God says that when He has spent His wrath, they will know that He, the LORD, has spoken in His zeal (Ezekiel 5:13). The words come from the LORD Himself. He says it right there.

Ezekiel, the priest and prophet living among the exiles (Ezekiel 1:1-3), is the one acting out the sign. But the verse points past him. God says they will know that He, the LORD, has spoken in His zeal (Ezekiel 5:13). The message is from the LORD.

That's right. God says she will be "…a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror to the nations around you…" (Ezekiel 5:15). It's a hard picture. It goes with Him executing judgments in anger, wrath and raging fury.

I'd love to hand you a shelter here, but the verse says otherwise. God says she will be "…a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror to the nations around you…" (Ezekiel 5:15). It's a heavy list. The nations are watching it happen.

That's not what the verse says, friend. God says she will be "…a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror to the nations around you…" (Ezekiel 5:15). It's a heavy word. He ends it with, "I, the LORD, have spoken."
True. God says, "I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will leave you childless." (Ezekiel 5:17) It's a heavy verse. I think it's one to take slowly.
This one is true, friend. God says, "I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will leave you childless." (Ezekiel 5:17) Plague, bloodshed and a sword come too. It's a heavy verse.
